articles.title: Grandma's First Tablet
articles.text:
Last week, my uncle bought Grandma a tablet for her seventieth birthday. "It's too hard for me," Grandma said. "I'm too old for these things." But we didn't give up.
Every afternoon this week, I became Grandma's little teacher. Day one: how to turn it on and make the words bigger. Day two: how to take photos. She took thirty photos of her flowers! Day three: video calls. When Uncle's face appeared on the screen, Grandma laughed like a young girl. "I can see you! Can you see me?" she shouted. She didn't need to shout, but it was so cute.
Now Grandma uses her tablet every day. She watches cooking videos, looks at our family photos, and video calls her sister in Kaohsiung every night.
"I was wrong," Grandma told me yesterday. "You are never too old to learn something new." I'm so proud of my student!

questions.q: Why did Grandma get a tablet?
options: It was her seventieth birthday gift.
She won it in a game.
questions.answer: It was her seventieth birthday gift.

questions.q: What did Grandma learn on day three?
questions.answer: Video calls.

questions.q: What did Grandma say yesterday?
options: "You are never too old to learn something new."
"The tablet is too hard for me."
questions.answer: "You are never too old to learn something new."

articles.title: The Day the Wi-Fi Died
articles.text:
Yesterday at noon, the internet at our home stopped working. No videos, no online games, no music. My sister and I looked at each other. "What do we do now?" she asked.
Dad called the internet company. They said, "We can fix it tomorrow morning." Tomorrow?! A whole day without Wi-Fi?
At first, we walked around the house like two lost cats. Then Mom took out an old box. Inside, there were board games, cards, and puzzles from years ago. We played a card game called Big Two. My sister won three times and danced around the sofa.
After dinner, we did a five-hundred-piece puzzle of a night sky and chatted about everything — school, funny dreams, our next trip. We didn't finish the puzzle, but nobody wanted to stop.
The Wi-Fi came back this morning. I'm happy about that. But you know what? Last night was the most fun night of this summer.

questions.q: What happened at noon yesterday?
options: The internet at home stopped working.
questions.answer: The internet at home stopped working.

questions.q: What was inside Mom's old box?
questions.answer: Board games, cards, and puzzles.

questions.q: How does the writer feel about last night?
options: It was the most fun night of this summer.
It was the most boring night ever.
It felt like a normal night.
It was scary without the internet.
questions.answer: It was the most fun night of this summer.

articles.title: A Message to the Wrong Person
articles.text:
My classmate Nina told me a funny and scary story about her weekend.
On Saturday, Nina wanted to send a message to her best friend Emma. She typed: "Math homework is so boring! Teacher Lin gives too much homework. I want to sleep in class!" Then she pressed send.
One second later, her face turned white. She didn't send it to Emma. She sent it to... Teacher Lin! Their names start with the same letter, and she picked the wrong name.
Nina wanted to hide under her bed forever. But ten minutes later, Teacher Lin replied: "Ha ha, I know it's a lot. But the test is coming. Sleep early tonight, and you won't want to sleep in class. 😊"
Nina says she learned two things. One: Teacher Lin is much kinder than she thought. Two: always check the name twice before you press send!

questions.q: Who did Nina want to send the message to?
questions.answer: Her best friend Emma.

questions.q: Why did she send it to the wrong person?
options: The two names start with the same letter, and she picked the wrong one.
questions.answer: The two names start with the same letter, and she picked the wrong one.

questions.q: How did Teacher Lin reply?
options: In a kind and funny way.
questions.answer: In a kind and funny way.

articles.title: Movie Night at Home
articles.text:
Every Friday night is movie night in our family. We don't go to the theater. We make our own theater at home!
Here is how we do it. First, we vote for the movie. This week, my sister and I wanted an animal cartoon, and Dad wanted a space movie. Mom had the last vote... and she chose the cartoon. Dad said, "Next week, space. You promised!"
Then we prepare the room. We turn off all the lights, put big pillows on the floor, and Mom makes a mountain of popcorn. Dad always adds too much butter, but nobody says no.
The movie was about a penguin who couldn't swim. We laughed, and near the end, Mom cried a little. (She always cries in movies!)
A theater ticket costs money, but our movie night is free — and it has the best seats, the best snacks, and the best people in the world.

questions.q: When is movie night in the family?
options: The first day of each month.
questions.answer: Every Friday night.

questions.q: What movie did they watch this week?
options: A cartoon about a penguin who couldn't swim.
A movie about a lost cat.
questions.answer: A cartoon about a penguin who couldn't swim.

questions.q: Who always cries in movies?
questions.answer: Mom.

articles.title: One More Level
articles.text:
"One more level, then I'll stop." I said this at eight o'clock. Then at nine. Then at ten. When Mom knocked on my door at ten thirty, I was still playing.
The game was so exciting. My character finally got the fire sword, and my team needed me. But Mom sat down next to me and asked one simple question: "Are you controlling the game, or is the game controlling you?"
I wanted to say "I'm controlling it," but then I looked at the clock. Three and a half hours passed, and it felt like thirty minutes. My eyes were dry. My homework wasn't done. Hmm. Maybe the game was winning — not just the level, but me.
So we made a deal: on game days, I set an alarm for ninety minutes. When it rings, I finish and stand up. It has been four days, and the alarm works. The fire sword is still there tomorrow. My time is not.

questions.q: What question did Mom ask?
options: "Are you controlling the game, or is the game controlling you?"
questions.answer: "Are you controlling the game, or is the game controlling you?"

questions.q: How long did the writer play that night?
questions.answer: Three and a half hours.

questions.q: What is the new deal?
options: Set an alarm for ninety minutes on game days.
questions.answer: Set an alarm for ninety minutes on game days.

articles.title: The Stranger Online
articles.text:
Last month, my cousin Ella got a message in her game app. It said: "Hi! You play so well! I'm Amy, 13, from Taichung. Let's be friends!" Ella was happy to have a new friend. They chatted about games and music every day.
Then "Amy" started asking strange questions. "Which school do you go to? Send me a photo! What is your address? I want to send you a gift." Ella felt something was wrong. Why does a new friend need her address?
Ella told her mom. Her mom said, "Good job telling me. On the internet, you can't see who is really behind the screen. A person who says they are 13 may not be 13."
Together, they blocked and reported the account. The game company later removed it — it was a fake account, and "Amy" wasn't a kid at all.
Ella still plays games and makes online friends. But now she has a golden rule: real friends don't need your private information.

questions.q: What made Ella feel something was wrong?
options: "Amy" asked for her school, photo, and address.
questions.answer: "Amy" asked for her school, photo, and address.

questions.q: What did Ella and her mom do?
options: They blocked and reported the account.
questions.answer: They blocked and reported the account.

questions.q: What is Ella's golden rule now?
options: Real friends don't need your private information.
Only chat with people from Taichung.
Always send photos to new friends.
questions.answer: Real friends don't need your private information.

articles.title: A Day Without Screens
articles.text:
Yesterday, our family tried a challenge: one whole day without screens. No phones, no TV, no computers — from morning to night. Dad put all our devices in a basket on top of the fridge.
The morning was the hardest part. My hand kept looking for my phone, like a habit. My sister touched the empty table where the tablet usually sits and sighed.
But slowly, the day filled up by itself. We made pancakes and ate them slowly. I finished a whole comic book. In the afternoon, we rode bikes to the river and flew a kite. My sister taught our dog to give a high five — it took her two hours, and it worked!
At night, we sat on the balcony, ate watermelon, and counted stars. Dad told us about his childhood without smartphones. "We were never bored," he said. "The world was our screen."
One day was enough for me to see it: screens are fun, but they eat time quietly. Now I want a screen-free day every month.

questions.q: Where did Dad put all the devices?
options: In a basket on top of the fridge.
questions.answer: In a basket on top of the fridge.

questions.q: What did the sister teach the dog?
questions.answer: To give a high five.

questions.q: What does the writer want now?
questions.answer: A screen-free day every month.
